synthesis.headline: Offshore gale lifts into New England today; a stronger Thanksgiving coastal storm follows with interior snow
synthesis.narrative:
The East Coast storm track organizes the week. Today's piece is the non-tropical gale center a few hundred miles east of North Carolina, analyzed as a 1009 mb low. It is yesterday's coastal low off northeast Florida, and NHC gives it near-zero development odds. It will reach southeastern Canada by Monday evening. Rain covers the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic today and the Northeast tonight. WPC has a Slight rainfall risk around Rhode Island and southeastern Massachusetts, and expect heavy surf and coastal flooding. Inland, a cold front runs from the Great Lakes through Arkansas to a 1011 mb low near the Texas-Oklahoma line and on into south Texas. SPC's only severe area is a Marginal risk in South Texas this afternoon, with MLCAPE of 1000-1500 J/kg and isolated hail, plus a Slight rainfall risk on the lower Texas coast. No mesoscale discussions are active. Behind the front, a 1028 mb high over the Great Basin and Rockies brings dewpoints in the teens and 20s. The Northwest gets rain and mountain snow from a Pacific front.

At 500 mb, a broad trough covers the central and eastern US, with heights near 540 dam over the Great Lakes. A jet with a core near 80 kt runs from the Plains to southeastern Canada. The trough tilts positive to neutral, so the strongest lift stays north and Texas storms stay isolated. A cold, possibly closed low over the Southwest drives a 45-55 kt southern branch to the Gulf. WPC expects more upper energy to bring snow to the central and southern Rockies Monday. Satellite shows a comma-wrapped trough off British Columbia that keeps sending Pacific systems into the Northwest.

A stronger storm follows. WPC expects a southern-stream disturbance to build a coastal low Wednesday, with heavy rain from South Carolina to the Virginia Tidewater, a Slight rainfall risk on the Carolina coast and gusts above 40 kt. On Thanksgiving the low strengthens as it moves north, bringing heavy rain and damaging winds to the I-95 corridor. Minor to moderate snow is possible from the central Appalachians into interior New England through Friday. Confidence drops from Thursday on because it depends on when the northern and southern streams merge. Pacific lows keep hitting the Washington-to-northern California coast all week. CPC's 6-10 day outlook favors northern-tier warmth (70-80% odds in Minnesota) and leans cool on the Gulf Coast. At 8-14 days, ensembles put a deep trough over the Gulf of Alaska and northwest flow into the central US.
synthesis.climate_context: El Niño is very strong and still growing. The Oceanic Niño Index for August-October is +2.46 °C, up every season from -0.21 in January-March, though the table gives no issue date. Strong El Niño winters usually bring an active subtropical jet, wet storms along the Gulf and Southeast coasts, and mild weather across the northern tier. This week fits that pattern: repeated southern-stream coastal lows and CPC's warm-north, cool-Gulf outlook. The Atlantic hurricane season ends November 30. NHC expects no tropical development in the Atlantic or eastern Pacific over the next seven days. The latest PNA, AO and NAO values are from October 31, too old to use.
synthesis.regional_notes: Lake-effect snow showers are expected over Michigan's Upper Peninsula and northern Lower Peninsula tonight into Monday. A Freeze Watch covers western Texas for Monday, after Freeze Warnings in southern New Mexico and southeastern Arizona. Dense Fog Advisories cover the Lower Mississippi Valley and Gulf Coast this morning. Monday, Atlantic easterly flow brings showers and storms to South Florida. Winter Weather Advisories are posted for the Northwest and northern California mountains. Day 2 has a Marginal rainfall risk for western Washington and the Olympic Peninsula.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary:
This 1200Z Sunday 22 November 2026 analysis shows a progressive, fairly modest pattern. The deepest low is in the far northwest corner near the Gulf of Alaska coast at roughly 990 mb, and the strongest high is over the Great Basin and central Rockies near 1028 mb, with a second 1026 mb high over the central Plains. A weaker 1015 mb low sits over the northern Plains and Upper Midwest, and a 1009 mb low with a trailing front is moving off the Carolinas, with a 1008 mb low just south of it offshore of the Southeast coast.

The most organized frontal feature is a cold front running from the Great Lakes low southwest across Missouri and Arkansas into northeast Texas, where a 1011 mb low sits on the boundary near the Texas-Oklahoma line. It continues as a cold front into south Texas, and it appears to turn stationary or warm-frontal east of the Lakes and across the Appalachians, where the front is hard to follow. Off the Southeast coast the cold front trails south from the 1009 mb low into the Atlantic and then curves back across Florida and the Gulf; a stationary or weakly defined boundary also lies across the northern Gulf Coast. In the West, a cold front sweeps down the California coast behind the Pacific system, with another cold front extending southwest from the Gulf of Alaska low across the Pacific Northwest.

The tightest gradients are in the northwest, around the Gulf of Alaska low and along the Pacific Northwest coast, and across the northern Plains between the 1028 mb Rockies high and the lower pressure to the east. The Great Lakes and Mid-Atlantic have moderate packing near the low and ahead of the front. Gradients are slack over the Southwest, the Gulf Coast, and the interior Southeast.

Lift and moisture are focused along the Texas-to-Great Lakes cold front, especially near the 1011 mb low, where southerly flow ahead of the boundary carries Gulf moisture north and dewpoints in the 50s and 60s are plotted across the Lower Mississippi Valley. A second moisture and lift zone runs along the East Coast frontal system near the 1009 mb low, with clustered precipitation symbols there. Behind the fronts, dewpoints drop into the teens and 20s across the Plains and Rockies, marking the dry continental air mass.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary:
This CMC surface analysis, valid 00Z Sunday 22 November 2026, is drawn on a polar projection, so the top of the frame is the high Arctic and Canada occupies the lower-middle portion. The dominant feature is a large, deep cyclone at the far left, with a closed centre of 964 mb and a second low near 973 mb to its north. Its tightly packed isobars and trailing cold front, which sweeps south and then curves back toward the lower left, place it over the far-left (Pacific/Alaska-side) part of the domain. I cannot confirm from the chart alone exactly which coastline sits beneath the centre, so I locate it by its position at the left edge rather than naming a region.

Over the Canadian interior, the chart is dominated by high pressure. A 1031 mb centre lies in the central part of the country, with 1023 mb and 1021 mb highs just northwest of it and a broad cold-air ridge extending south. Lows of 1016 mb and 1015 mb sit near the highs' southern flank over the Great Lakes/Hudson Bay region, though the geography there is hard to resolve at this scale, so I treat that placement as approximate. Gradients here are weak, consistent with a cold, quiescent interior.

Cross-border, a 994 mb low sits in the western United States, near the left-centre of the lower half, with an associated front and a 1005 mb low farther south over the central US. A cold front runs from a 1009 mb low northeast of the Great Lakes down through the eastern US toward a 1005 mb low in the southern Plains, marking the principal frontal boundary connecting Canadian cold air to US systems. Farther east, a 1001 mb low near the Quebec/Atlantic side carries a front trailing southward along the eastern seaboard.

In the high Arctic and over Greenland, a string of lows (990 to 1013 mb) and highs (1020 to 1027 mb) lie across the top of the frame, with a pair of 987 mb and 992 mb lows and fronts at the right edge near the Greenland/North Atlantic sector. These are plausible for the Arctic at this time of year and are not unusual on their own.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary: The 1200 UTC 22 Nov 2026 analysis shows a large-scale trough over the central and eastern CONUS with the heights falling to roughly 5,400 m (540 dam) near the Great Lakes and upper Midwest, while the flow over the Pacific Northwest and Canadian Rockies is ridged, with 5,400-5,440 m contours (540-544 dam) bulging poleward along the northwestern edge of the chart. A broad closed-looking low sits over the southern Rockies and Southwest, with the heights near 5,700 m (570 dam) at its southern flank. The contours around it appear to wrap the center, but the nearest contour I can read confidently is the 570 dam line, so I would call it a deep, cold cutoff candidate rather than assert complete closure from the chart alone. In the Great Lakes and Ohio Valley region the 500 mb flow is strongly confluent with the tightly packed contours and a mostly southwesterly flow ahead of the trough. The shaded isotach field shows a jet streak of roughly 55-70 kts, with a secondary maximum approaching 80 kts, stretching from the central Plains through the Great Lakes and angling northeast toward the Northeast and southeastern Canada, with the strongest winds shaded near the top right of the chart. Another weaker band of 45-55 kts wraps around the base of the southwestern low, from southern California and Arizona into Texas and the Gulf Coast. Over the Southeast and Atlantic coast, heights are near 5,730-5,780 m (573-578 dam) and the flow is weak, which is consistent with a modest ridge or a trough-ahead-of-ridge arrangement there. The overall pattern shows a quasi-stationary ridge along the northwestern edge of the chart, a cutoff-like low over the Southwest, and a progressive trough in the East, rather than a classic Rex block, because no anticyclone is plainly poleward of the southwestern low at the same longitude. The tilt of the eastern trough appears to be slightly positive to neutral, with the axis running from the upper Midwest toward the Southern Plains, though the exact tilt cannot be pinned down without the full chart.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary:
The most organized feature is a long, north-south band of dry orange-brown air with a narrow cloud band along its eastern edge, running from the Upper Midwest and western Great Lakes southward through the Mississippi Valley toward the Gulf Coast. This sharp dry-to-moist contrast is the likely jet corridor in the eastern half of the country, and the cloud band along it looks like a cold front with a thin line of mid-level cloud. A second dry tongue sweeps from the central Plains into Oklahoma and northern Texas, and the dry air also reaches across the northern Plains into the Dakotas, so this orange-red field lies on the cyclonic side of the western trough rather than under a ridge.

Farther west, the plotted pattern is a deep trough or closed low off the Pacific Northwest and British Columbia coast, shown by the saturated purple and magenta swirl at the upper left with a comma-shaped cloud band wrapped around it. The purple tones mean cold, dry upper-tropospheric air, and the cloud streamers extending southeast across Oregon, Idaho, Nevada and into the Rockies mark the downstream flow from that system. The dry orange tongue on the east flank of the trough near the northern Plains is the most plausible stratospheric-intrusion candidate, though the image alone shows dryness, not descent.

On the Atlantic side, a compact, very bright cloud shield sits off the Mid-Atlantic coast, east of the Delmarva and Virginia area. It looks like a small area of deep convection or a developing offshore low, with a long cloud tail trailing southwest along the Carolina coast to the northwest Bahamas. A larger cluster of deep convection sits over the western Atlantic southeast of the Bahamas, north of Hispaniola and Puerto Rico, with scattered tops near the Greater Antilles.

The Gulf of Mexico, Florida, Cuba and the Yucatan are dominated by green, indicating tropical moist air with little organized convection. A band of dry orange air across the northern Gulf contrasts with the deeper green to the south.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary: This 13:10Z GOES-19 Air Mass composite on 22 November shows a broad swath of green tropical moist air across the Caribbean, Central America, northern South America and the tropical eastern Pacific, with the most vigorous deep convection in the Atlantic and southern Brazil rather than in the tropics proper. A compact white cloud mass sits north of Hispaniola and the Bahamas around 25N, east of Florida, and further north a bright cloud shield and comma-like cloud band curve off the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast coast, with a white blob offshore. That curved band, along with the blue-to-purple corridor arcing across the Canadian Maritimes and the North Atlantic, marks a sharp airmass boundary that implies a jet corridor running northeast; the purple and dark blue to its north and west are cold, dry upper-tropospheric air. Across Canada and the Arctic edge of the disk, purple and reddish-brown shades north of the Great Lakes and over Hudson Bay mark dry air on the cyclonic side of the flow, though the extreme viewing angle there limits detail. Over the tropical Pacific, only scattered convective clusters appear, with a few bright cells near 100-110W and thin cirrus streaks near Central America; there is no organized tropical wave or cyclone evident. South of the equator, the large bright convective complex over southern Brazil and Paraguay near the Uruguay border stands out as the strongest tropical-side feature, while orange-brown dry air with cloud bands wraps the southeastern Pacific and the Southern Hemisphere frontal zone off Chile and Argentina.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary:
The outlook for November 27 - December 1 favors above-normal temperatures across most of the contiguous US. The strongest signal is over the northern tier: a core of 70-80% odds covers Minnesota and the eastern Dakotas, surrounded by 60-70% from Washington and Montana through the Plains and Upper Midwest, with similar 60-70% odds over southern California and western Arizona. Probabilities relax to 50-60% across the interior West, Southwest, central Plains, and Ohio Valley, then to 33-50% along a southwest-to-northeast band running from southern Texas through the Mid-Mississippi and Ohio Valleys into the Mid-Atlantic and southern New England.

The cool side is confined to the Gulf Coast: a swath of leaning-below-normal (33-40%) odds from the Texas coast through Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia and the Florida Panhandle and northern peninsula. A near-normal zone separates it from the warm signal, spanning the Carolinas, Tennessee Valley, and interior Texas. Alaska leans above normal, strongest over the eastern interior and Panhandle. Hawaii leans below normal.

The map shows probabilities of tercile category, not temperature departures, and no height fields are plotted, so any statement about the upper-level pattern is inference. The gradient is sharp and oriented southwest to northeast, with high-confidence warmth in the north and a cool or near-normal signal along the Gulf Coast and Southeast. That geometry is consistent with a ridge over the western and north-central US and a trough or at least cooler flow near the Southeast, though the chart does not show the flow itself.

Because the warmth is strongest and most widespread across the northern tier, with the signal weakening toward the Gulf and Atlantic coasts, the outlook implies the current regime persists into the 6-10 day window rather than breaking down. The cool Gulf Coast signal is the one piece suggesting some Southeast trough influence, but its low probabilities mean it is a weak lean, not a confident forecast.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is the CPC 6-10 day 500 mb height and anomaly outlook (made 21 Nov 2026, valid Nov 27 to Dec 1) on a polar stereographic projection. Solid green contours are heights, labeled in meters (5100 to 5880 m, i.e. 510 to 588 dam), and dashed lines are anomalies at 60 m (6 dam) intervals. The labels on the dashed lines (30, 90, 150, 210 and so on) are in meters, not dam, so the strongest positive center reads 210 m, about +21 dam, and the contours cluster as nested red rings.

The dominant feature is a large positive anomaly over the Arctic Ocean north of the Canadian Archipelago and Greenland, peaking near +21 dam (210 m) just north of the Canadian Arctic islands, with a second +21 dam center toward the top right of the chart. Its sign is opposite to the deep negative height anomaly (a 510 dam closed low, 5100 m) over the Canadian Arctic and Baffin Island region, where anomaly values reach roughly -9 to -12 dam (blue dashed lines, labeled -90 and -100 m). A second negative center lies over Greenland and the northeast Atlantic near -9 dam (labeled 90 and 150 m, with the sign carried by blue dashes), and a broad negative area spans Alaska and the Gulf of Alaska toward the western edge, around -3 to -9 dam.

Over western North America the anomaly pattern is modest. A weak positive zone (red dashes, roughly +3 dam or less) sits over the Pacific Northwest and the Canadian prairies, and the zero line (purple dashed) runs through the interior West and curves back toward the southern Rockies and the Gulf of Mexico. Weak negative anomalies (about -3 dam) cover the south-central U.S. and Gulf Coast. The implied picture is of positive anomalies retreating poleward and shrinking, with the strong positive center displaced to high latitudes rather than anchored over western North America.

The height contours show a nearly zonal pattern across the continental U.S., with the 5580 to 5820 m lines running west-southwest to east-northeast, and a trough dug into northeastern Canada. There is no strong ridge axis over the West; the weak ridging appears as a gentle northward bulge of the contours in the Pacific Northwest. The flow therefore looks more zonal and less amplified over the contiguous U.S., while the amplified, high-latitude blocking-like anomaly pair (positive Arctic, negative Baffin and Greenland) holds the amplification farther north.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is the CPC 8-14 day 500 mb height and anomaly outlook (valid Nov 29 - Dec 5, 2026), though the labels need careful reading: the solid green contours are heights labeled in meters (5280, 5460, 5640, and so on, i.e. roughly 528-564 dam), and the dashed lines are anomalies at 60 m intervals per the legend. At that interval the dashed values read 30, 90, 150 (red, positive) and -30, -60, -120 (blue, negative) in meters, so these are departures of roughly 3 to 15 dam, with the largest positive values plausible only as ensemble-mean departures near the pole. I have some doubt about the exact numbers because the labels are sparse and partly clipped.

The dominant feature is a large trough over the North Pacific and western Alaska, with a blue negative-anomaly center of about -120 m (12 dam) near the Gulf of Alaska/Bering side of the domain and a second negative center near -120 to -60 m in the far northwest corner. Heights run lower than normal along the entire Pacific coast of Canada and Alaska. A second, comparable negative center sits over the North Atlantic east of Labrador and Greenland (about -120 m), with another to its southeast.

A broad positive anomaly dominates the Arctic and the Canadian Arctic Archipelago, with red contours rising from 30 to 90 to 150 m toward the pole, and the zero-anomaly (purple) line wraps around the continent. Over western Canada, the northern Rockies and the northern Plains the pattern is mixed: the 30 m line hugs the Pacific Northwest and southern British Columbia coast, but the interior of the northern Rockies and Plains lies near the zero line or slightly negative, with a blue negative anomaly closed off over the central and southern Plains. The positive anomaly is therefore weak and confined to the extreme northwest of the lower 48 and Canada, not a ridge core over the northern Rockies.

The contour geometry supports that reading. The height contours bow sharply northward over the eastern Pacific and western Canada, then dive southeastward across the Plains and Midwest, so mean flow is northwesterly over the central U.S., consistent with a ridge axis lying offshore or along the coast rather than inland. At the southwest edge of the chart a red 30 m contour appears off Baja California and the Southwest, suggesting modest positive anomalies there, but this is at the margin of the domain and I would not call it a ridge core retreat with confidence.

Net: a strongly negative Pacific trough, a positive Arctic anomaly, and mean troughing over the central and eastern U.S., with the ridge axis west of the Rockies rather than centered over them.

sources.title: Excessive Rainfall Outlook (Day 1)
sources.summary: This Day 1 outlook, valid 12Z Sunday Nov 22 to 12Z Monday Nov 23, 2026, shows only the two lowest categories, Marginal (green) and Slight (the legend's orange category, drawn here as an orange contour), with no Moderate or High areas. The Slight risk appears in two small spots: one on the south Texas coast, where a yellow-filled patch sits near the Rio Grande Valley south of the Corpus Christi area, and one in southern New England, an orange contour around what looks like Rhode Island and the adjacent southeastern Massachusetts coast. The yellow fill on the Texas patch does not match the legend's orange Slight color, so I read it as the same Slight category but with some uncertainty. The Marginal risk is a broad green band along the Gulf coast of Texas wrapping around the Slight patch, and a long narrow green strip hugging the Northeast coast from near the Mid-Atlantic coast northward through New Jersey, southern New England and into Maine. Both Slight areas, the highest category drawn, sit inside their Marginal envelopes. The elongated, coast-parallel shape of the Northeast strip fits a frontal or coastal-low setup, while the compact Texas coastal area suggests onshore flow or a boundary near the coast, but the chart alone cannot confirm a tropical system, front or terrain forcing, and it shows risk categories only, not rainfall amounts.

sources.title: Excessive Rainfall Outlook (Day 2)
sources.summary: This Day 2 Excessive Rainfall Outlook, valid 12Z Monday November 23 through 12Z Tuesday November 24, 2026, shows a single risk area: a small green Marginal (at least 5%) region labeled MRGL. It sits over the far northwestern corner of the Lower 48, covering the Olympic Peninsula and the coastal and western Washington lowlands, and appears to extend toward Puget Sound and the northern Washington coast. No Slight, Moderate or High risk areas are drawn anywhere, and the rest of the country, including the Gulf Coast, Southeast and Northeast, is left blank, meaning no excessive rainfall risk is outlined there. Marginal is the lowest category, so the signal is for isolated rather than widespread flash-flood concerns. The pattern is consistent with a Pacific system moving into the Northwest coast, though the chart shows only risk categories, not the rainfall forcing. The chart alone gives no way to say how this compares with a Day 1 outlook for the same event, so I would not claim the risk has grown or relaxed.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary:
As of 258 AM EST Sunday, November 22, 2026:

Excessive rainfall: Slight Risk (level 2/4) over New England on Sunday, and over the western Gulf Coast and southern Texas with a front and thunderstorms through Monday morning.

Eastern storm: A low over the Southeast moves north into southeastern Canada by Monday evening. Rain falls over the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic Sunday, then spreads into the Northeast Sunday night into Monday, ending Monday evening. Isolated thunderstorms are possible in the Southeast early Sunday. Monday, Atlantic easterly flow brings showers and storms to the southern tip of Florida.

Front: Extends from the Upper Midwest to the Southern High Plains, moving east off the Northeast coast by Monday evening. It brings rain Sunday from the Upper Midwest to the Middle Mississippi Valley, and dissipates over the Central Appalachians by Tuesday.

Cold and fog: High pressure builds over the Central and Southern Rockies Sunday evening. Freeze Warnings were in effect for southern New Mexico and southeastern Arizona through early Sunday, and a Freeze Watch covers western Texas for Monday. Dense Fog Advisories cover the Lower Mississippi Valley and Gulf Coast.

Snow: Cold high pressure over the Upper Midwest brings lake-effect snow showers to the Upper Peninsula and northern Lower Peninsula Sunday night into Monday.

West: A Pacific Northwest front reaches the Great Basin and dissipates late Sunday, bringing rain and higher-elevation snow to the Northwest and Northern California, with Winter Weather Advisories. Snow spreads into the Northern Intermountain Region, Northern Rockies, and Sierras. Monday, upper-level energy brings snow and lower-elevation rain to the Central and Southern Rockies.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary:
SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook, issued 6:56 AM CST Sunday, November 22, 2026, valid 1300Z November 22 to 1200Z November 23.

Marginal risk of severe thunderstorms across South Texas, mainly during the afternoon and early evening. Rich low-level moisture and modest heating should bring MLCAPE to about 1000-1500 J/kg. Large-scale lift from the departing shortwave will be displaced north, so only isolated storms are expected, along the south/southeast-advancing cold front and possibly ahead of it near the coast. Deep-layer shear is sufficient for organization, so isolated severe hail is possible with the strongest storms. Locally strong wind gusts are possible but limited, since low-level flow is very weak and upscale growth is not expected.

Farther north, from the ArkLaTex into western Tennessee and Kentucky, isolated diurnal storms may form along the front. MLCAPE reaches only 500-750 J/kg, so severe potential is limited. A few stronger storms could occur in the mid to late afternoon, especially across southern and eastern Arkansas.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: No SPC mesoscale discussions have been issued in the past six hours, so no organized convective threat is currently under active monitoring by the Storm Prediction Center. The product carries no forecast content or hazard details for this period. Because mesoscale discussions are short-fuse products issued when a watch is being considered or a specific area needs close attention, their absence means SPC is not flagging an imminent localized severe-weather or convective-scale concern. This does not rule out severe weather. Broader outlooks and any watches issued separately would need to be checked for threats over longer time horizons.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
As of 700 AM EST Sunday, November 22, 2026, the Atlantic has no tropical cyclone development expected. A non-tropical, gale-force low a few hundred miles east of the North Carolina coast is producing disorganized showers and thunderstorms. It is forecast to move north into unfavorable conditions, so tropical or subtropical development is not expected. Formation chances are near 0 percent through both 48 hours and 7 days. Regardless of its status, the system is expected to bring heavy rain, gusty winds, dangerous surf, rip currents, and coastal flooding to parts of the eastern U.S. coast over the next couple of days. Gale Warnings are in the National Weather Service High Seas Forecasts.

As of 400 AM PST Sunday, November 22, 2026, tropical cyclone formation is not expected in the eastern and central North Pacific east of 180 degrees longitude during the next 7 days.

sources.title: NHC Active Storm Advisories
sources.summary: NHC currently lists no active tropical cyclones in any basin, and no advisories are being issued. The product gives no as-of time, so this status should be treated as unverified for the exact moment of the briefing.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary:
The Oceanic Niño Index shows a strengthening El Niño. The latest value listed, for the ASO 2026 season, is an anomaly of +2.46 °C, which is in the very strong El Niño range. The SST total for that season is 29.23.

The anomaly has risen every season in the table, from -0.21 in JFM 2026 (La Niña-leaning, near neutral) through +0.11 (FMA), +0.46 (MAM), +0.95 (AMJ), +1.39 (MJJ), +1.80 (JJA), and +2.16 (JAS). The rise is steady, though the SST total is levelling off, rising only 0.11 from JJA to ASO.

The product gives no as-of date, so the currency of the latest season cannot be confirmed from the table alone.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary:
Teleconnection indices, latest daily values dated 2026-10-31. The product warns that all three are STALE (the newest value is 22 days old) and should not be treated as current.

PNA: +0.57 on 10-31, turning positive after late-October readings near -0.6. Seven-day mean -0.24, down from +0.06 the prior week (falling).

AO: +0.77 on 10-31, positive but easing. Seven-day mean +1.03, down from +1.44 (falling).

NAO: +1.15 on 10-31, the highest value in the window, after a low of -0.79. Seven-day mean +0.59, up from +0.26 (rising).

The product describes these as summer indices, where extratropical teleconnections are weaker. Treat them only as directional support.
